sections.heading: 2.3 Time, Velocity, and Speed

blocks.text: There is more to motion than distance and displacement. Questions such as, “How long does a foot race take?” and “What was the runner’s speed?” cannot be answered without an understanding of other concepts. In this section we add definitions of time, velocity, and speed to expand our description of motion.

sections.text: There is more to motion than distance and displacement. Questions such as, “How long does a foot race take?” and “What was the runner’s speed?” cannot be answered without an understanding of other concepts. In this section we add definitions of time, velocity, and speed to expand our description of motion.

sections.heading: Time

blocks.text: As discussed in Physical Quantities and Units, the most fundamental physical quantities are defined by how they are measured. This is the case with time. Every measurement of time involves measuring a change in some physical quantity. It may be a number on a digital clock, a heartbeat, or the position of the Sun in the sky. In physics, the definition of time is simple—time is change, or the interval over which change occurs. It is impossible to know that time has passed unless something changes.

The amount of time or change is calibrated by comparison with a standard. The SI unit for time is the second, abbreviated s. We might, for example, observe that a certain pendulum makes one full swing every 0.75 s. We could then use the pendulum to measure time by counting its swings or, of course, by connecting the pendulum to a clock mechanism that registers time on a dial. This allows us to not only measure the amount of time, but also to determine a sequence of events.

How does time relate to motion? We are usually interested in elapsed time for a particular motion, such as how long it takes an airplane passenger to get from his seat to the back of the plane. To find elapsed time, we note the time at the beginning and end of the motion and subtract the two. For example, a lecture may start at 11:00 A.M. and end at 11:50 A.M., so that the elapsed time would be 50 min. Elapsed time Δt is the difference between the ending time and beginning time,

sections.heading: 2.3 Time, Velocity, and Speed
sections.text: Motion has more parts than distance. It also has displacement. We need more ideas to answer some questions. For example, how long does a foot race take? What was the runner's speed? We need new words to describe motion. These words are time, velocity, and speed. They help us explain motion better. Understanding these concepts is necessary. It helps answer questions about duration. It also helps answer questions about speed.

sections.heading: Time
sections.text: We define basic things by how we measure them. Time is one of these things. Measuring time means seeing a change. This change can be a number on a clock. It can be a heartbeat. It can be the Sun's position in the sky. In physics, time is change. It is the interval over which change occurs. You cannot know time passed if nothing changes. We measure time by comparing it to a standard. The SI unit for time is the second. We write this as s. A pendulum may swing once every 0.75 s. We can count these swings to measure time. We can also link it to a clock. This helps us measure time amounts. It also helps us see the order of events. How does time link to motion? We often care about elapsed time. This is the time for a specific motion. For example, how long does it take to walk to the back of a plane? To find elapsed time, we note the start time. We also note the end time. Then we subtract the start from the end. A lecture may start at 11:00 A.M. It may end at 11:50 A.M. The elapsed time is 50 min. Elapsed time Δt is the end time minus the start time.
